Pilot Sample Sizes for Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Standardized Mean Difference

Source: R/seq_mr_smd.R
seq_mr_smd_pilot.Rd

Returns the pilot (first stage) sample size for each group in the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) procedure of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) for the standardized mean difference. It needs only the cost constants, so it can be computed before any data are collected.

Usage

seq_mr_smd_pilot(A, c, m_0 = 4, gamma = 0.49)

Arguments

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. The article builds it as the amount one is willing to pay to estimate the standardized mean difference to within \(\epsilon\), divided by \(\epsilon^2\) (for example \(2500 / 0.5^2 = 10000\)). A single positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation: a single positive number when an observation costs the same in both groups, or two positive numbers, c(c1, c2), the cost in group 1 and the cost in group 2, in that order. Either group may be the costlier one.

m_0

The smallest pilot size allowed per group: a whole number of at least 4 (the default), as in the article.

gamma

The tuning constant of the stopping rule's correction term, strictly between 0 and 1/2. The default, 0.49, is the value Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) suggest. Use the same value in seq_mr_smd.

Value

When c is a single number, a length one integer: the pilot size for each group. When c has two elements, an integer vector with names group_1 and group_2.

Details

With one cost for both groups the pilot size per group is Equation 14 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017), $$m = \max\left\{m_0,\ \left\lceil (A/(2c))^{1/(2 + 2\gamma)} \right\rceil\right\}.$$ The article's examples give 13 for \(A\) = 10,000 and \(c\) = 2.40 (p. 105), and 30 for \(A\) = 50,000 and \(c\) = 1 (p. 102).

With two different costs the pilot sizes are Equations 20 and 21 of the article ("A General Scenario", p. 106). Writing \(c_1\) for the smaller cost and \(c_2\) for the larger, the less costly group starts with $$m_{1} = \max\left\{m_0,\ \left\lceil (A/c_1)^{1/(2 + 2\gamma)} \right\rceil\right\}$$ observations and the costlier group with $$m_{2} = \max\left\{m_0,\ \left\lceil m_{1} \left(1 + \frac{(c_2 - c_1)\,m_{1}^2}{A}\right)^{-1/2} \right\rceil\right\}.$$ For \(A\) = 50,000 and costs of 2 and 8 these are 30 and 29. The article assumes the first group is the less costly one; this function accepts the costs in either order and returns the sizes in the order of c.

Equation 20 uses \(A/c_1\) where Equation 14 uses \(A/(2c)\), so the article's two cost pilot does not reduce to its one cost pilot when the costs are equal. When the two costs supplied are equal this function returns the one cost (Equation 14) size for both groups. Two costs count as equal when their relative difference is at most the square root of machine precision (about 1.5e-8), so that costs computed by arithmetic (24 * 0.1 against 2.4) are not sent to the two cost procedure by rounding error; the smaller of the two is then the cost used.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2017). Estimating the standardized mean difference with minimum risk: Maximizing accuracy and minimizing cost with sequential estimation. Psychological Methods, 22(1), 94–113. doi:10.1037/met0000089

See also

seq_mr_smd for the stopping rule and seq_mr_smd_sensitivity to study the procedure before collecting data; in DMAR, mr_smd (the one cost procedure) and the fixed sample size planner ss_aipe_smd.

Other seq_mr_smd: seq_mr_sensitivity, seq_mr_smd()

Author

Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in, Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The worked example of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017, p. 105): assessing
# one student costs 2.40 dollars, and the team would pay 2,500 dollars to
# estimate the standardized mean difference to within 0.5.
seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 2500 / 0.5^2, c = 2.40)
#> [1] 13

# Two costs: an observation in the second group costs four times as much.
seq_mr_smd_pilot(A = 50000, c = c(2, 8))
#> group_1 group_2 
#>      30      29
